**Module 3 objectives**

This module introduces widely used techniques for analysing multivariate biological data. By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Understand the principles underpinning **Principal Components Analysis (PCA)** and **Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (nMDS)**
- Be familiar with the concepts behind **multivariate hypothesis testing** using **permutational techniques** such as **ANOSIM** and **PERMANOVA**
- **Plan and conduct experiments** that test multivariate hypotheses
- Perform these analyses using relevant software tools (**Jamovi**, PRIMER, or R)
- **Interpret, present, and report** the results of multivariate analyses effectively

:::

## Introduction

In this practical, you will:

- Use **PCA** to analyse "lecturer perceptions" data collected in previous years
- Work in groups to **design an investigation** using a model system to **test a multivariate hypothesis** for your upcoming report

Please read the [Introduction to Module 3](301-intro.qmd) for an overview of the methods and activities covered in this module.

## Part 1: Principal components analysis – “perceptions of biology lecturers”

**Principal Components Analysis (PCA)** is a technique used to **reduce the dimensionality** of a dataset by extracting a smaller set of **new variables (principal components)** that capture as much of the **variance** in the original data as possible. These components summarise complex patterns across multiple variables, making the data easier to visualise and interpret.

You will use PCA to reduce your set of measured variables to a coherent, smaller dataset. In addition, you will compare perceptions of lecturers across groups defined by preferred system (marine, freshwater or terrestrial), preferred taxon (animals or plants) and gender (male or female), using conventional univariate approaches (t-tests/ANOVAs). To perform these univariate approaches, make sure that you not only create the principal components (PCs) but also save the scores (see below) for each component.

### Run the PCA

**The process in JAMOVI is listed below. R instructions are given on Canvas in an R script file.**

1. Import your data. [**Download the Week 9 PCA data file**](canvas:/files/50497754/download?download_frd=1). If the direct download does not work, open [**Module 3 Resources on Canvas**](canvas:/pages/module-3-resources) and download the file there.
   - Open **Jamovi**.
   - Go to the top-left menu (☰) → click **Open** → **Browse** and select your Excel/csv file (e.g., your lecturer dataset).

![Video showing how to open the Week 9 lecturer dataset in jamovi.](assets/w09-jamovi-load-data.mp4)

Set the 21 lecturer-rating variables, from **accessible_approachable** to **well respected in their field**, to **Continuous** (look for a ruler icon in the column headers). Leave **gender**, **main organism** and **main system** as **Nominal**.

To change the rating variables together, go to the **Variables** tab, select them, then click **Edit** and set **Measure type** to **Continuous**. The video below shows how to do this for the lecturer dataset.

![Video showing how to set the lecturer-rating variables to Continuous in jamovi.](assets/w09-jamovi-variables-continuous.mp4)

2. Run Principal Components Analysis.
   - Go to **Analyses → Factor → Principal Component Analysis**.

3. Select your variables.
   - Select the 21 lecturer-rating variables and click the arrow to move them into **Variables**. Check that you have left out the student ID and the grouping columns.

![Video showing how to open Principal Component Analysis and move the lecturer-rating variables into the analysis.](assets/w09-jamovi-run-pca.mp4)

Some options may already be selected by default. Check that your settings match those below, and change them where needed.

4. Method.
   - Check that **Varimax** is selected in the **Rotation** dropdown. The rotated loadings will appear in the **Component Loadings** table.

5. Assumption Checks.
   - Check that **Bartlett’s test of sphericity** is ticked (to help assess whether the data are suitable for PCA).

6. Number of Components.
   - Select **Based on eigenvalue** and check that **Eigenvalues greater than** is set to **1** (Kaiser’s criterion). Change this only if you have a specific reason to do so.

7. Additional Output.
   - Check that **Component summary**, **Initial eigenvalues** and **Scree plot** are ticked.

![Video showing how to set the PCA options in jamovi.](assets/w09-jamovi-pca-options.mp4)

8. Save component scores.
   - Open **Save** and check that **Component scores** is ticked.
   - Go to the **Data** tab and scroll to the right to find the new columns: **Score Component 1**, **Score Component 2**, and so on.

![Video showing how to save component scores and view the new columns in the Data tab.](assets/w09-jamovi-save-component-scores.mp4)

9. Check your data and results.
   - Check the rating columns for missing entries before interpreting your results.
   - jamovi updates the results as you change the settings, so wait for it to finish before reading the tables.

10. Produce the correlation matrix.
   - Go to **Analyses → Regression → Correlation Matrix**.
   - Select the same 21 lecturer-rating variables and click the arrow to move them into the analysis.
   - Under **Correlation Coefficients**, check that **Pearson** is ticked.

### Review the output

- **Correlation Matrix**: Check for variables that are not correlated with the others. These may not be suitable for PCA — you can remove them and rerun the analysis if needed.
- **Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity** tests whether your correlation matrix is significantly different from an identity matrix—a matrix where all off-diagonal values are zero (no correlation between variables), and all diagonal values are one (each variable only correlates with itself). Bartlett’s Test should be significant (p < .05): a **significant result** means that your correlation matrix is not an identity matrix, and PCA ***can*** be used. That said, this test is most useful when used **alongside visual inspection** of your correlation matrix. If many variables aren’t correlated with others, they may not contribute much to PCA and could be removed.
- **Scree Plot**: Helps determine how many components to retain.
- **Rotated Solution**: Makes it easier to interpret your components.
- **Saved Scores**: You can now use these component scores in further analyses (e.g., regression or cluster analysis).

### Interpret the components

You need to:

- Look at the correlation matrix.
- Examine the scree plot and determine how many PCs you can identify (eigenvalues >1, Kaiser’s Criterion).
- Establish a meaningful name for each component based on the loadings for individual variables in the rotated solutions.

### Compare groups using component scores

Examine whether gender, system biases (marine v. terrestrial) and taxon (animal v. plant) biases may affect the perceptions of biology lecturers. You can use the text labels already in **gender**, **main organism** and **main system** for the group comparisons. Check that these columns are set to **Nominal**; there is no need to recode them as numbers.

For an independent-samples t-test, go to **Analyses → T-Tests → Independent Samples T-Test**. Put the saved component scores into **Dependent Variables** and the relevant nominal grouping column into **Grouping Variable**. Under **Tests**, untick **Student’s** and tick **Welch’s** if the assumption of equal variances is not met.

Questions to consider:

- Do males and females perceive lecturer qualities the same way?
- Do botanists and zoologists perceive lecturer qualities the same way?
- Do marine and terrestrial folk perceive lecturer qualities the same way?

## Part 2: Designing your multivariate experiment

### The data and your model system

Biologists are increasingly turning to **multivariate approaches** because the questions we ask—and the data we collect—are often inherently multivariate. This is especially true when studying both biotic **assemblages** and **abiotic habitat variables**.

To explore these analytical techniques, you will work in groups to generate your own multivariate datasets using **non-biological model systems**. Examples include:

- **Cars** and the **car parks** they inhabit
- **Gargoyles** and the **buildings** they reside on
- **Beer types** and the **drinking establishments** in which they appear

These creative analogues allow you to test and visualise multivariate patterns in a controlled and accessible way.

#### Example: cars as a model system

Cars have been successfully used as a teaching model for ecological analysis (e.g., Gaston et al. 1993). In this context:

- Different car **types** can be treated as "**species**".
- Different **suburbs** or **locations** represent "**sites**".
- The car park **characteristics** (e.g., size, surface, signage) act as "**habitat variables**".

A sample proforma is provided to illustrate how such a system can be structured to generate a multivariate dataset with **testable hypotheses**. Download the blank project-planning proforma and the completed car-park example from the [Project-planning downloads](#project-planning-downloads) section below.

### Group work

As a group, you will:

- **Design your own non-biological multivariate model system.**
- Develop 2–3 testable hypotheses relating to:
  - The **assemblages** of "species" across different **treatments** (e.g., locations, types of environments);
  - The role of measured "**habitat variables**" in shaping those assemblages.
- Use a **two-factor design** where possible (e.g., site × time, or suburb × establishment type).
- Ensure adequate replication—you will need at least 3 replicates per treatment.
- Design a **sampling strategy** that allows you to collect the required data.
- **Assign a data coordinator within your group to manage dataset preparation.**

### Project-planning downloads

- [Download the blank project-planning proforma (Word)](assets/w09-project-planning-template.docx){download="w09-project-planning-template.docx"} and type your group's plan into the document.
- [Download the completed car-park example (Word)](assets/w09-project-planning-example.docx){download="w09-project-planning-example.docx"} for guidance on completing the proforma.

## Week 10 group presentation (compulsory)

During the **Week 10** practical session (**next week**), your group will deliver a brief presentation (<5 minutes) using a PowerPoint presentation to introduce your project.

This session is **compulsory** and designed to provide constructive feedback before you begin data collection. Don’t worry—feedback is friendly and intended to improve your design, not critique your creativity! **There are no marks allocated for this presentation.**

Your presentation should include:

- An **introduction** to your system (model species and treatments)
- Your 2–3 hypotheses
- A description of your **taxonomy** (how you're classifying your “species”)
- Your **sampling design**, including sample size and sampling effort
- A list of **habitat variables** you will measure at each site (and how you will measure them)
- A simple **map of your sites**

## Install *miso* for next week {#install-miso}

*miso* (Multivariate Inference, Similarity and Ordination) is a jamovi module developed by us to facilitate the analysis of multivariate data. It is freely available and can be installed manually using a downloaded `.jmo` file.

If you prefer not to use R and the `vegan` package, or are unable to obtain a licensed copy of PRIMER, *miso* provides a convenient alternative within jamovi.

We will use *miso* in next week’s practical to analyse community data. If you have time during today’s practical, install it now. Otherwise, install it at home before your next practical.

### Install the module

1. Go to the *miso* [GitHub releases page](https://github.com/usyd-soles-edu/miso/releases).
2. Scroll to the latest release (usually at the top of the page) and choose the `.jmo` file for your operating system (Windows or macOS). macOS users have two options: Intel or Apple Silicon. If you are unsure, check your Mac’s specifications.
3. Download the file to a location you can easily access (e.g., your Desktop or Downloads folder).
4. Open jamovi, select the **Analyses** tab if needed, then click **Modules** in the top-right corner.
5. In the Modules window, select **jamovi library → Sideload**, then click the large grey upload icon.
6. In the file browser pop-up, navigate to the location where you saved the `.jmo` file, select it, and click **Open**.
7. A "Module installed successfully" message will appear. After installation, check that a new **Multivariate** section appears under **Analyses** in jamovi.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Default

![Installing *miso* in jamovi.](assets/w09-jamovi-install-miso.mp4)

#### Warm tint

![Installing *miso* in jamovi.](assets/w09-jamovi-install-miso-manila.mp4)

:::

That is it! You are now ready to use *miso* in next week’s practical.

## Report 1 overview {#assessment-overview}

To give you the maximum opportunity to analyse your data and understand your results, your group’s dataset will be checked during Week 11 by demonstrators.

### Group data submission (5%)

- This is a group assessment: only one group member needs to upload the data file (Excel format) to Canvas on behalf of the group.
- The dataset must be submitted before your Week 11 practical session.
- It is worth 5% of your total unit mark.
- Near-perfect datasets that are well-organised, correctly formatted, and ready for analysis will receive the full 5%.
- As this is a group submission, Special Consideration, Simple Extensions, and Academic Plans do not apply.

### Individual report (15%)

Each student will submit an individual short report, focusing primarily on the Methods and Results sections, as outlined in the attached marking rubric.

- **The report must include:**
  - A brief Introduction with clearly stated hypotheses
  - A detailed Methods section, describing your data collection and analyses
  - A well-presented Results section with appropriate tables, figures, and descriptions
- You are not required to invent a detailed rationale or references for your study, although you are welcome to include them if you wish.
- Your report must be written in the format of a manuscript suitable for submission to Austral Ecology.
- Length limit: Maximum of **four single-spaced pages**
  (not including the cover sheet, title/abstract page, references, tables, or figures)
- Emphasis will be placed on:
  - Clear explanation of analytical methods
  - Accurate description of the data collected
  - Clear and concise presentation of results

## Report submission details

Your individual report is due by **23:59 on 6 November 2026**. Please ensure it is submitted electronically and anonymously via Canvas.

We aim to return reports with summative feedback approximately one week after submission.

### Academic integrity

You are expected to complete your report independently and uphold the principles of academic honesty.

- Plagiarism or copying from others will result in loss of marks and may lead to further disciplinary action.
- Refer to the University’s policies on academic integrity: [Academic Integrity at the University of Sydney](https://www.sydney.edu.au/students/academic-integrity.html)

### Use of ChatGPT or similar tools

- You may use tools like ChatGPT to check grammar or assist with R coding.
- However, extensive use of AI to write your report will be detectable and penalised. We are looking for your own scientific reasoning and interpretation.

### Report format

Your report should follow the format of a short scientific article suitable for submission to Austral Ecology. The “Notice to Contributors” is available at: [Austral Ecology – Author Guidelines](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/page/journal/14429993/homepage/ForAuthors.html)

:::
